sources.title: Sec. 37.15 — Reporting Obligations; Licensing (S.F. Admin. Code ch. 37)
sources.quote:
Owners of residential dwelling units subject to this Chapter 37 shall be required to report certain information about their units to the Rent Board, as set forth in subsections (b) and (c).

If a landlord has substantially complied with the obligation to report information about a rental unit as required under this Section 37.15, the landlord shall receive a license to impose rent increases on tenants in that unit under Sections 37.3(a)(1)-(2). If the landlord has not substantially complied with the reporting obligation, then the license to impose rent increases shall be temporarily suspended during the period of the landlord’s noncompliance. Upon receipt of the required information from the landlord, the suspension shall be terminated, and the license to impose rent increases shall be restored prospectively, but a tenant shall not be obligated to pay the increased rent for months during the period of suspension.
sources.used_for: The rent increase licence: who must hold it, how it is obtained, and the consequence of not holding it.

sources.title: Sec. 37.3 — Rent Limitations (S.F. Admin. Code ch. 37)
sources.quote:
(1) Annual Rent Increase. A landlord who has reported the required information about their rental unit to the Rent Board as set forth in Section 37.15 shall have a license to impose annually a rent increase which does not exceed a tenant’s base rent by more than 60% of said published increase.

(2) Banked Rent Increases. A landlord who refrains from imposing an annual rent increase or any portion thereof may accumulate said increase and, subject to Section 37.15, impose that amount on the tenant’s subsequent rent increase anniversary dates.

(5) Nonconforming Rent Increases. Any rent increase which does not conform with the provisions of this section shall be null and void.

(A) Except as provided in Section 37.3(a)(11)(B), a landlord may not impose increases solely because a tenant has added an additional occupant to an existing tenancy, including, but not limited to, a newborn child or family member as defined in Section 401 of the Housing Code.

Ord. No. 3-26, effective February 9, 2026

sources.title: The Rent Board Housing Inventory — and the rent increase licence
sources.quote:
Property owners who report that a unit is tenant-occupied will receive a rent increase license that allows them to impose annual allowable and banked rent increases.

A landlord must have a current rent increase license on file with the Rent Board before any annual or banked rent increase can go into effect. The rent increase license does not need to be included with your rent increase notice.

The information entered in the housing inventory submission is public.

sources.title: Banked rent increases
sources.quote:
A skipped increase is only banked if at least 24 full months pass without any rent increase. If less than 24 months pass, the skipped increase is lost and cannot be imposed at a later date.

Banked increases do not have to be approved by the Rent Board, but must be calculated correctly. They cannot be compounded or prorated.

sources.title: Learn about rent increases in San Francisco
sources.quote:
The allowed rent increase percentage in San Francisco is 1.6%.

The percentage is effective March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027.

Landlords must calculate the rent increase on the tenant’s base rent only. This includes any housing services like parking or storage. It does not include any temporary passthroughs or fluctuating charges.

Rent increases cannot be rounded up to the nearest dollar.

The landlord should use the percentage that will be in effect on the date of the increase, not the percentage in effect on the date they serve the notice.

sources.title: Rent Board Rules and Regulations, Part IV — §§4.10 (Notice) and 4.12 (Banking)
sources.quote:
(a) A landlord who refrains from imposing an annual rent increase, or any portion thereof, may accumulate said increase and impose that amount on or after the tenant's subsequent rent increase anniversary date; however, the rent may be increased only one time every twelve (12) months. This banked amount may only be given at the time of an annual increase. A full 12 months must have elapsed from the date that an annual rent increase, or a portion thereof, could have been imposed before this banking section becomes applicable. Banked increases shall not be compounded and shall not be rounded up.

(b) In order to impose an accumulated rent increase the landlord shall: (1) inform the tenant, on or before the date upon which the landlord gives the tenant legal notice, which portion of the rent increase reflects banked amount, and (2) the dates upon which said banked amount is based; provided, however, that failure to include such information shall not render the increase null and void.

sources.title: Rent Increases Under Section 6.14 and Costa-Hawkins
sources.quote:
Rules and Regulations Section 6.14 provides for an unlimited rent increase on remaining occupants when the last original occupant vacates the unit, as long as the landlord timely served all remaining occupants with a written "6.14 notice."

The 6.14 notice must be served on each subsequent occupant within a reasonable time after the landlord knows or should have known of the occupancy. Generally, sixty days is considered reasonable. A 6.14 notice can be served on any subsequent occupant, whether the subsequent occupant is a subtenant or a co-tenant.
sources.used_for: What an occupant change does and does not allow: the §6.14 notice, the sixty-day reasonableness benchmark, and the co-tenant versus subtenant distinction.

sources.quote:
Section 6.14 requires the service of a written notice upon the subsequent occupant when he or she first moves into the unit. Such notices are not a prerequisite to a Costa-Hawkins rent increase.

A landlord is not required to file a petition with the Rent Board for approval of a rent increase pursuant to Section 6.14 or Costa-Hawkins Section 1954.53(d). sources.title: Rent Board Rules and Regulations: Part XIII — Reporting Obligations
sources.quote:
A landlord who has substantially complied with their obligation to report information about a rental unit as described above shall receive a license to increase rent for that unit under Ordinance Sections 37.3(a)(1)-(2). Any rent increase under Ordinance Sections 37.3(a)(1)-(2) purporting to be effective while the landlord is unlicensed shall render the entire rent increase null and void; provided, however, that the effective date of the rent increase, not the date of service, shall be used to determine whether or not the increase conforms with the provisions of this section. Nothing in this Regulation shall affect a landlord’s banking rights or the ability to accumulate otherwise lawful rent increases that were found to be null and void.

This section shall apply to all rent increases that are effective on or after July 1, 2022, except that with respect to condominium units and buildings with less than ten residential units, this section shall only apply to rent increases that are effective on or after March 1, 2023.

sources.title: General Obligation Bond Passthrough Worksheets
sources.quote:
Different tenants in the same property may have different passthrough rates, depending on when they moved into the property.

The landlord is not required to file a petition with the Rent Board for approval of the Bond Measure Passthrough. However, the landlord must use the Bond Measure Passthrough Worksheet in order to calculate the passthrough. To impose the passthrough, a copy of the completed Worksheet must be provided to the tenant in addition to a written notice of rent increase.

The passthrough must be imposed at the time of the annual rent increase, on the tenant’s rent increase anniversary date. It does not become part of the tenant’s base rent, and it must be discontinued after the tenant has paid the passthrough for the number of months specified on Line 8 of the passthrough worksheet.

licensing_steps.question: Does a single individual owner (no corporation) need a rent increase licence?
licensing_steps.answer: Yes. The duty is written for "owners of residential dwelling units subject to this Chapter 37" and the Housing Inventory page states that all owners of residential property must report, including units in buildings with fewer than 10 units and condominiums. There is no small-owner or individual-owner exemption.

licensing_steps.question: Is the licence an application that the Rent Board approves?
licensing_steps.answer: No. It is generated automatically when the owner reports the unit in the Housing Inventory with a tenant in occupancy: "Property owners who report that a unit is tenant-occupied will receive a rent increase license". Reporting is free and is done online in the Rent Board Portal. No approval, hearing or fee is involved.

licensing_steps.question: Does the owner have to send the Rent Board the rent increase notice, or ask permission for the annual or banked increase?
licensing_steps.answer: No for ordinary annual/banked increases: banked increases “do not have to be approved by the Rent Board,” and the tenant notice is not filed with the Board for approval. The Board-facing duty is Housing Inventory reporting. Certain increases above the annual/banked route require a landlord petition; general obligation bond and water revenue bond passthroughs use required worksheets instead of an approval petition, and certain utility passthroughs have their own worksheet/petition route.

licensing_steps.question: When must the licence exist?
licensing_steps.answer: A current licence must be on file before any annual or banked increase "can go into effect". It does not have to be attached to the notice, but it must be live on the effective date. The reporting deadline is 1 March every year; for a building with fewer than 10 units, reporting began on 1 March 2023.

licensing_steps.question: What happens if the unit was never reported?
licensing_steps.answer: The license is “temporarily suspended” while the owner is not in compliance. Filing restores it prospectively; it does not retroactively validate an increase that took effect while unlicensed. Rule 13.14 says an annual or banked increase imposed without a current license is null and void, while the underlying banking rights are preserved. Do not rely on a later filing to cure past unlicensed months.

licensing_steps.question: Is the licence the same thing as the annual Rent Board fee?
licensing_steps.answer: No. The license is free and comes from the Housing Inventory report. The Rent Board Fee is separate: $59.00 per dwelling unit for the 2026–2027 tax year, due March 1 unless exempt. After full payment, up to 50% may be recoverable only from tenants in occupancy on the applicable November 1; penalties are not recoverable. Keep any recovery separate from base rent. Requesting a fee exemption does not satisfy Housing Inventory reporting.

licensing_steps.question: Can a tenant check whether the owner holds a licence?
licensing_steps.answer: Yes. The Rent Board states that a tenant can search the Rent Board Portal to see whether the landlord is up to date. The Housing Inventory information reported by owners is public.

licensing_steps.question: Is the Rent Board licence the only licence an individual owner needs?
licensing_steps.answer: There is a second, separate City registration that is often confused with it. The Business Registration Certificate is issued by the Office of the Treasurer & Tax Collector as a general business-tax registration. Do not treat one registration as satisfying the other. The Housing Inventory asks for a business registration number “if any”; the Rent Increase License still comes from substantial Housing Inventory compliance.

licensing_steps.question: Does this owner need a Business Registration Certificate?
licensing_steps.answer: Not established from the brief. If this is one residential structure with fewer than four units and rental income is the only business activity, Business and Tax Regulations Code §853(d) says that fact alone does not require a certificate. The brief supplies two rent-controlled units, not the total unit count in the structure or other business activity. Confirm those facts before relying on the exception; do not infer a two-unit building from two reported units.

licensing_steps.question: When would a Business Registration Certificate become required?
licensing_steps.answer: The exception is conditional. Other San Francisco business activity, payroll expense, or short-term residential rental income can trigger registration; the Tax Collector determines the actual unit count. The “Qualified Lessor” gross-receipts exclusion is a narrow nonprofit-managed limited-partnership definition, not a blanket individual-owner exemption. This is logged as H-21 and must be confirmed against the owner’s records and, if needed, the Tax Collector.

process_steps.action: Confirm coverage, unit count, and subsidy status
process_steps.detail: The reported 1940 construction meets the date test on its face, but coverage/exemptions and the total number of units in the structure are not established. Two reported rent-controlled units do not prove a two-unit building. Check the certificate of occupancy, exemption categories, and any government subsidy.

process_steps.action: Reconcile leases and the full rent ledger
process_steps.detail: Use signed leases, amendments, every notice, and payment records. Unit 1’s $3,995.00 is reported again on April 1, 2026; its fixed-term status is unknown. Unit 2’s $3,150.00 is only the June 1, 2019 lease-start input; current base and prior increases are unverified.

process_steps.action: Report/update the Housing Inventory and confirm both licenses
process_steps.detail: Complete reporting before notice as the safer sequence. The hard gate is a current license on the increase’s effective date. Save dated portal evidence and recheck on that date. Late filing restores prospectively only.

process_steps.action: Check the separate Treasurer business-registration question
process_steps.detail: Determine the actual structure unit count and other business activity. The fewer-than-four-units-in-one-structure exception may apply only on those facts; do not treat the Rent Board license or fee as business registration.

Use the published allowance in effect on the effective date and proven banked components, added without compounding or rounding up. Re-check Legistar File #261020 before any large catch-up; it is pending, not law. Leave unsupported passthrough amounts blank.

process_steps.action: Screen retaliation, fair housing, repairs, and lease authority
process_steps.detail: Review protected activity, repair requests/petitions, protected-class selection, harassment risk, and fixed-term clauses. A neutral method helps; it is not a safe harbour.

process_steps.action: Choose the effective date and notice period
process_steps.detail: One increase every 12 months. Civil Code §827 requires 30 days at ≤10% and 90 days above 10%, measured against the prior 12 months; California mail adds five calendar days. Do not use the multiple-year page’s 30/35-day shorthand for a >10% increase.

process_steps.action: Prepare the itemized notice and any required worksheet
process_steps.detail: State dollar amount, percentage, effective date, annual/banked split, and banked basis dates. A bond passthrough needs the completed worksheet and anniversary notice; fee recovery is separate from base rent. No draft notice is attached to this repository.

process_steps.action: Serve, retain proof, and recheck the license
process_steps.detail: Use personal delivery or mail under Civil Code §827 and CCP §1013. Keep dated proof of service and confirm the license remains current on the effective date.

process_steps.action: Keep annual reporting and the separate fee current
process_steps.detail: Report into the Housing Inventory by March 1 each year and pay the Rent Board Fee if due. Any fee recovery must satisfy its own occupancy/payment conditions and remain separate from base rent.

notice_rows.item: Required — written notice served on the tenant
notice_rows.detail: Personal delivery or mail under Civil Code §827 and CCP §1013; keep dated proof.
30 days at ≤10%; 90 days above 10%, measured against the prior 12 months. California-to-California mail adds five calendar days; longer extensions can apply elsewhere.

notice_rows.item: Required — dollar amount, percentage, and effective date
notice_rows.detail: Use the rate in effect on the effective date, not merely the service date.
Identify the annual portion and any banked portion. Rule 4.10(b) and 4.12(b) contain text-specific exceptions; include the information rather than litigate an omission.
State the dates on which the banked amount is based. Rule 4.12(b) expressly says omission does not itself void the increase, but the safe practice is to include them.

notice_rows.item: Required — current license on the effective date
notice_rows.detail: The license need not be attached, but an unlicensed annual/banked increase is null and void under Rule 13.14; late filing restores prospectively only.

If a general obligation bond passthrough is imposed, provide the completed worksheet with the written notice, on the anniversary date; it is temporary and not base rent. No amount is established here.
If a unit is government-subsidized, check the program’s own notice/approval rules. Subsidy status is unverified; no program-specific amount or procedure is inferred.

notice_rows.item: Recommended — calculation schedule and proof of service
notice_rows.detail: Attach or retain a clear calculation schedule and dated service evidence. This is a risk-control recommendation, not a claim that every attachment is statutorily required.

notice_rows.item: Recommended — plain-language explanation and contact route
notice_rows.detail: Explain the legal component and provide a contact route for questions. Do not promise attorney approval or guaranteed acceptance.

notice_rows.item: Prohibited — retaliation, protected-class selection, or bad-faith pressure
notice_rows.detail: A facially correct percentage does not cure an unlawful motive or harassment.
Do not add rent solely because an additional occupant joined; a separate cost petition is a different, unproven route.

reasons.detail: Use the allowance in effect on the effective date, once every 12 months, on base rent only.
Add supported percentages without compounding or rounding up; itemize the banked portion and basis dates. Re-check pending File #261020 before a large catch-up; it is not law.

No approval petition, but a completed worksheet, actual tenancy-commencement year, net taxable value, unit count, anniversary notice, and temporary non-base charge are required. No dollar amount is established here.
After full fee payment, up to 50% may be recoverable from qualifying November-1 occupants; penalties are not recoverable. Do not fold it into base rent.
Certain utility passthroughs require a worksheet filed before notice or a petition; no utility facts or amount are established here.
A landlord petition and supporting documentation are required before the tenant notice; no capital-improvement facts are established here.
A landlord petition is required; ordinary cost increases are not a self-help annual surcharge.
A Board petition is required; market rent alone is not a lawful sitting-tenant increase.

reasons.reason: Market pressure or portfolio pricing software
reasons.lawful: Not a lawful basis by itself
reasons.detail: Market pressure does not override the ordinance. SF prohibits covered algorithmic devices using nonpublic competitor data; the DOJ RealPage matter is an enforcement example, not proof of universal corporate behavior.
Retaliation, protected-class discrimination, and bad-faith pressure to vacate remain unlawful even with correct arithmetic.
A roommate-only surcharge is unlawful even if the lease purports to allow it.

practice_rows.corporate: Same ordinance, same percentage, same notice rules.
practice_rows.individual: Same ordinance, same percentage, same notice rules — no small-owner exemption in Chapter 37.

practice_rows.corporate: Required, obtained from the annual Housing Inventory report.
practice_rows.individual: Required, obtained from the annual Housing Inventory report; free and automatic.

practice_rows.corporate: Banned in San Francisco: no algorithmic device using non-public competitor data to set rents or occupancy.
practice_rows.individual: Banned as well; the prohibition is on "a landlord", and tenants and tenant nonprofits may sue.

practice_rows.corporate: DOJ allegations and a proposed RealPage settlement document concerns about shared nonpublic competitor data in portfolio-scale pricing tools; they do not establish typical behavior by every corporate landlord.
practice_rows.individual: No official dataset measures how individual SF owners set increases. The verified statement is the rule set, not a behavioural average.

practice_rows.corporate: The AB 1482 exemption for single-family homes and condominiums is unavailable to a REIT, a corporation, or an LLC with a corporate member.
practice_rows.individual: An individual owner may qualify for that exemption — but it is irrelevant to these units, which are already under SF's lower local cap.

practice_rows.topic: Records that make an increase defensible
practice_rows.corporate: No official source establishes a universal corporate recordkeeping practice. A documented per-unit ledger, neutral policy, notice, and service evidence are prudent controls.
practice_rows.individual: Use the same per-unit evidence discipline: lease, full ledger, license evidence, coverage, calculation, notice, and proof of service. This is a recommended checklist, not an exhaustive statement of every legal duty.

practice_rows.corporate: Must evaluate Treasurer business registration on the actual facts; corporate form does not replace Housing Inventory reporting.
practice_rows.individual: Same analysis. The fewer-than-four-units-in-one-structure exception depends on total unit count and other business activity, not merely on being an individual owner.

practice_rows.corporate: Same current law; monitor pending File #261020 before serving.
practice_rows.individual: Same current law; the proposed 10% cap is pending, not enacted, and is not applied to current arithmetic.

fair_housing_rows.point: Is a difference between the two units itself unlawful?
fair_housing_rows.finding: No provision in the cited Chapter 37, Civil Code §1947.12, Government Code §12955 or the federal Fair Housing Act requires identical treatment. The prohibition is discrimination or harassment because of a protected characteristic.

Federal: race, colour, national origin, religion, sex, familial status, disability. California adds, among others, gender, gender identity and expression, sexual orientation, marital status, ancestry, source of income, veteran or military status, and genetic information.

fair_housing_rows.point: Is a discriminatory rent increase already harassment under local law?
fair_housing_rows.finding: Yes: §37.10B(a)(9) makes it bad-faith harassment to "violate any law which prohibits discrimination" in the protected categories it lists.

fair_housing_rows.point: What objective reasons justify different outcomes for the two units?
fair_housing_rows.finding: Use documented lease terms, verified current base rent, anniversary dates, and proven banked history. The brief supplies different lease-start dates and amounts, but Unit 2’s current base and both units’ complete histories are not verified.

Selecting a unit because of a protected characteristic; bad-faith pressure to vacate; retaliation under the conditions of Civil Code §1942.5; unresolved repair petitions; or a nonconforming notice. A 180-day complaint history is a review trigger, not an automatic bar.

fair_housing_rows.point: Is there an official safe-harbour rule for "treat both units the same"?
fair_housing_rows.finding: No official source states that raising both units identically cures a discrimination risk, or that raising one unit creates one. Both questions are decided on the reason for the difference, not on the pattern.
Civil Code §51 prohibits arbitrary discrimination by business establishments; housing-specific FEHA duties also apply. A neutral documented method is useful evidence, not immunity.

review_rows.evidence: Current lease and full ledger; Unit 2’s $3,150.00 is only a 2019 lease-start input.

review_rows.evidence: Every prior notice and payment record; one increase every 12 months.
Complete history satisfying the applicable banking tests; no compounding or rounding up.

review_rows.test: Is the notice period correct for the cumulative increase?

review_rows.test: Is there an actual conforming draft notice?
review_rows.evidence: No draft notice is attached to this repository. The skeleton is a review aid only.

review_rows.evidence: Repair requests, inspections, petitions, and protected activity; §1942.5 is fact-specific.

review_rows.evidence: No written policy was supplied. A recommended method is described, not certified as existing.

review_rows.evidence: Per-unit reasons, communications, and timing; identical percentages are not a safe harbour.

review_rows.evidence: Identify any revenue-management tool using nonpublic competitor data; no such use is established here.

flags.item: Banking guidance uses two measuring points; worked-example labels need care
flags.detail: Rule 4.12(a) reads in full: "A landlord who refrains from imposing an annual rent increase, or any portion thereof, may accumulate said increase and impose that amount on or after the tenant's subsequent rent increase anniversary date; however, the rent may be increased only one time every twelve (12) months. This banked amount may only be given at the time of an annual increase. Only those increases which could have been imposed on, or subsequent to, April 1, 1982, may be accumulated. A full 12 months must have elapsed from the date that an annual rent increase, or a portion thereof, could have been imposed before this banking section becomes applicable. Banked increases shall not be compounded and shall not be rounded up". The Rent Board's banking guidance page uses a different measuring point: "A skipped increase is only banked if at least 24 full months pass without any rent increase." Re-fetched 2026-11-08. For a tenancy reviewed annually both tests are satisfied by the Unit 1 scenario date, so this is not a proven legal conflict; the two formulations measure from different events.
flags.effect: The 1.4% component is not conditional on choosing between two rules. It remains conditional on the actual lease, anniversary, license, and ledger. Official worked-example year errors are separately logged H-19.
flags.action: Apply Rule 4.12(a) and the guidance together. Note the additional clause "This banked amount may only be given at the time of an annual increase", which is why banked amounts are combined with an annual increase rather than served alone. Verify dates from the ledger, not from the Rent Board's worked-example year labels (see H-19).

flags.detail: February 1, 2027 is a scenario based on the February 1, 2025 lease start and no intervening increase. The April 1, 2026 paperwork and full ledger were not supplied for review.
flags.effect: Any different last-increase date changes the anniversary, available bank, and notice calendar.
flags.action: Review the 2025 lease, April 2026 instrument, every later notice, and the complete rent ledger.

flags.detail: The 13.1% illustration assumes no increase after June 1, 2019. That is an assumption made for arithmetic, not an established owner statement or official fact.

flags.action: Produce the full rent ledger and every increase notice since June 2019 before using any banked amount.

flags.detail: Whether both units are current in the Housing Inventory was not checked; the record is held in the Rent Board Portal, which this session cannot access.

flags.item: Coverage not confirmed against official records
flags.detail: Year built 1940 satisfies the date test on its face, but coverage also depends on the unit not being in an exempt class (for example certain single-family or condominium situations).
flags.effect: If a unit is not covered, the local cap does not apply and the analysis changes entirely.

flags.detail: The analysis treats 1 April 2026 as a partial change of occupancy (an original tenant remained), so there is no vacancy reset and no additional-occupant charge.

flags.action: Keep the 2025 lease, the 2026 change documents, and proof of continuous occupancy.

flags.detail: The increase must be calculated on base rent, which includes housing services such as parking or storage and excludes temporary passthroughs.

flags.item: Retaliation and repair history require a fact-specific review
flags.detail: Section 1942.5 is not an automatic 180-day prohibition on every increase. It addresses retaliation under stated conditions, preserves lawful cause, and includes a good-faith-ground provision. Separately, a qualifying repair petition can defer an annual increase.
flags.effect: Protected activity, repair requests, inspections, disputes, and petition deadlines can create exposure even when arithmetic is correct.
flags.action: Review correspondence, complaints, inspections, rent status, lawful cause, repairs, and any petitions; obtain legal review if any exist.

flags.detail: No official source publishes a permissible or typical market increase for covered units in 94122. Commercial listing data is not an official source and was not used.
flags.effect: The value is left blank. The official ceiling is the only verified number.
flags.action: Treat the Rent Board allowance as the reasonableness benchmark.

flags.item: No official dataset on corporate vs individual owner behaviour
flags.detail: Official sources state the rules that bind every landlord; none measures how individual SF owners typically set increases.
flags.effect: Practice comparison is qualitative and cited to the ordinance, not to statistics.
flags.action: None required; do not rely on industry averages.

flags.item: Service dates are computed, not official
flags.detail: The dates add the statutory period to the intended effective date, with 5 extra days for mail under Code of Civil Procedure §1013.
flags.effect: Weekends, holidays and proof of service can move the last safe date.
flags.action: Serve well before the last date and keep proof of service.

flags.item: The 13.1% scenario is neither a certified maximum nor a reasonableness finding
flags.detail: The additive arithmetic is reproducible on $3,150.00, but the current base and no-prior-increase premise are unverified. Official banking guidance does not supply a ZIP-specific business recommendation to take the whole amount at once.
flags.effect: The amount may change completely after the ledger review. Any phase-in choice is a separate lawful-neutral business decision, not a legal safe harbour.
flags.action: Do not serve a 13.1% notice from this illustration. Verify all inputs first, then document a neutral decision.

flags.item: Notice-defect consequences are text-specific, not universally void
flags.detail: Section 37.3(b)(5) states a null-and-void rule. Rule 4.10(b) contains an exception where the amount is no more than allowable annual plus banked increases, and Rule 4.12(b) expressly says omission of banked dates does not itself render the increase null and void.
flags.effect: It is inaccurate to say every itemisation omission automatically voids an otherwise valid increase. The conservative course remains full itemisation.
flags.action: State the annual and banked dollar amounts, percentages, effective date, and banked basis dates; do not rely on an exception.

flags.item: Owner's premise partly incorrect: no per-increase filing with the Rent Board
flags.detail: The owner believed the Rent Board must be informed of, or must license, each increase. The licence is real but comes from the annual Housing Inventory report; annual and banked increases "do not have to be approved by the Rent Board".
flags.effect: The compliance step is the annual report, not a filing about the increase.
flags.action: Report by 1 March each year; serve a conforming notice for each increase.

flags.item: Unit 1 fixed-term versus month-to-month status is unknown
flags.detail: The April 1, 2026 continuing-tenancy instrument was not supplied. Official California guidance says rent cannot be increased during a fixed term unless the agreement permits increases; renewal is another possible point.
flags.effect: A February 1, 2027 increase could be too early. If a fixed term runs through March 31, 2027 without an escalation clause, an April 1, 2027 scenario would use the not-yet-published 2027–28 rate; that rate cell stays blank.
flags.action: Read the signed instrument and any escalation/renewal clause before selecting an effective date.

flags.item: Unit 2 current base rent is not expressly supplied
flags.detail: The brief supplies $3,150.00 as the June 1, 2019 lease-start rent. It does not separately certify that this is the current base rent in November 2026.
flags.effect: The $50.40 annual-only and $412.65 combined figures are illustrations on that input, not verified current amounts or lawful maxima. Official current-base confirmation is blank.
flags.action: Verify the current base rent and its components from the lease and full ledger.

flags.item: Official Rent Board worked examples contain year-label errors
flags.detail: The current rent-increase page includes an example assigning 1.6% to June 1, 2025, and its multiple-year example contains inconsistent year labels. The banking page’s worked example later refers to August 1, 2024 while using the 2025 scenario. Form 571 controls the published periods and rates.
flags.effect: Do not copy example-year labels. The calculations here use Form 571 dates and independently recomputed arithmetic.
flags.action: Use Form 571 for every effective period and recheck the current official page before serving.

flags.item: Free tenant representation is not guaranteed by the referral listing
flags.detail: The Rent Board confirms that a lawyer is not required to file a petition and lists legal resources, including a Sunset office. The listing describes legal assistance and, for some providers, income or service-area limits; it does not promise every tenant free representation for notice review.
flags.effect: Tenants have official review routes, but availability, eligibility, scope, and capacity must be confirmed with each provider.
flags.action: Describe these as referral resources, not guaranteed free lawyers. Rent Board counseling and petitions remain available without counsel.

flags.item: Business Registration Certificate determination is conditional and rests on owner-supplied facts
flags.detail: Business Registration Certificate determination is conditional. §853(d) says rental income from one residential structure consisting of fewer than four units does not, by reason of that fact alone, require registration. The brief supplies two rent-controlled units, not the total structure unit count; other business activity, payroll expense, or short-term rental income can also trigger registration. The “Qualified Lessor” exclusion is nonprofit-LP-only.
flags.effect: Do not infer a two-unit building or a settled registration exemption from the two reported units.
flags.action: Confirm total units in the structure, other business activity, payroll, and short-term rental use; ask the Tax Collector if uncertain.

flags.item: Pending ordinance would cap banked increases at 10% per year — re-check before serving any large catch-up
flags.detail: Board of Supervisors File #261020 would amend the Administrative Code so that banked rent increases and capital improvement rent increases "may not increase a tenant's rent by more than a total of 10% per year, for the next three years". Re-checked on Legistar on 2026-11-08: Status "Pending Committee Action", introduced 2026-09-15, in the Land Use and Transportation Committee, sponsors Sauter, Chan and Mahmood, with no final action, no enactment date and no enactment number. It is proposed legislation, not law, and no figure in this repository applies it.
flags.effect: The Unit 2 scenario total of 13.1% exceeds 10%. If enacted as introduced, that catch-up could not be imposed in a single year. The annual allowable increase itself is unaffected.
flags.action: Re-check the Legistar record for File #261020 immediately before serving any banked catch-up above 10%, and phase a large banked amount over multiple years if it has been enacted.

flags.item: Whether a §6.14 notice was served on the occupant who joined Unit 1 in April 2026
flags.detail: A 6.14 notice must be served on each subsequent occupant within a reasonable time after the landlord knows or should have known of the occupancy; sixty days is generally considered reasonable, and Rule 6.14(d)(1) makes failure within 60 days of actual knowledge a rebuttable presumption of untimeliness. The reported change was 1 April 2026, so the benchmark fell around 31 May 2026. No notice, proof of service, or record of non-service was supplied for review.
flags.effect: If the owner later wants the §6.14 route when the last original occupant vacates, an untimely notice may bar it. Under Rule 6.14(d)(2) the Costa-Hawkins route may still be available even without a 6.14 notice, subject to its own limits.
flags.action: Locate any 6.14 notice and its proof of service, or record the date the owner first learned of the occupancy and why no notice was served.

flags.item: Whether the occupant who joined Unit 1 in April 2026 is a co-tenant or a subtenant
flags.detail: Costa-Hawkins does not reach a co-tenant who moved in after the original occupant, regardless of when they moved in; a co-tenant is someone with an oral or written agreement with the landlord, or whom the landlord has treated as a tenant by the acceptance of rent or other conduct. A 6.14 notice, by contrast, can be served on either a subtenant or a co-tenant.
flags.effect: The label does not change the current 1.6% scenario, but it decides whether any later market-rate reset is available and by which route.
flags.action: Check whether the April 2026 instrument added the occupant to the lease, and whether rent has been accepted directly from them.

flags.item: Bond passthrough inputs and amount are unverified
flags.detail: Actual tenancy commencement years, net taxable value, total unit count, and applicable worksheet factors are not established. The 2026–27 worksheet lists FY2018-19 = 0.0044 and FY2024-25 = 0.0041, but those factors apply only to actual commencement years. No passthrough dollar amount is calculated.
flags.effect: Any bond passthrough amount remains blank; do not add it to base rent or to the annual/banked scenarios.
flags.action: Obtain the tax bill, unit count, and lease commencement records; complete the official worksheet before any notice.

flags.item: Bond worksheet license phase-in date conflicts with Rule 13.14
flags.detail: The 2026–27 bond worksheet says the small-building/condominium requirement applies to increases effective on or after March 1, 2022. Rule 13.14 and §37.15 guidance say March 1, 2023. The worksheet also uses July 1, 2021 for larger buildings while the rule/guidance say July 1, 2022.
flags.effect: Do not copy the worksheet’s phase-in dates into the license analysis; use the rule and current guidance and ask the Board if a historical date matters.
flags.action: Flag the form irregularity and confirm with the Rent Board before relying on a historical phase-in date.

flags.item: Multiple-year guidance notice shorthand conflicts with Civil Code §827
flags.detail: The Rent Board multiple-year page says 30 days, or 35 if mailed, for any annual/banked increase. Civil Code §827 requires 90 days when the cumulative increase is greater than 10%, plus the applicable mail extension.
flags.effect: The 13.1% Unit 2 scenario uses the 90-day statutory band, not the page’s 30/35-day shorthand.
flags.action: Use Civil Code §827 and CCP §1013; flag the guidance conflict rather than silently copying it.

flags.item: Ordinance 3-26 effective-date discrepancy between convenience text and official publisher
flags.detail: The Board convenience compilation lists Ordinance 3-26 as effective February 9, 2026; American Legal, identified by the Board as the official publisher, lists Eff. 2/8/2026. The discrepancy does not change the current 1.6% rate or the conditional arithmetic.
flags.effect: Do not represent either date as silently reconciled; the official publisher is the code source, and the Board page is a convenience compilation.
flags.action: Use the official publisher for code text and ask the Rent Board to reconcile the convenience compilation.

occupancy_rows.situation: An original occupant is still in the unit
occupancy_rows.rule: Both routes are keyed to the last original occupant leaving. Section 6.14 requires that the last original occupant "vacate"; Costa-Hawkins requires that the last original occupant no longer "permanently reside" in the unit.
occupancy_rows.effect: On the reported facts one original Unit 1 occupant remained after 1 April 2026, so no market-rate reset is available and the 1.6% allowance governs. Continuous occupancy still needs documents (H-06).

occupancy_rows.situation: A new occupant joined while an original occupant remained
occupancy_rows.rule: A landlord may not charge more rent solely because an additional occupant joined, even if the lease or rental agreement provides for the additional charge.
occupancy_rows.effect: Unit 1 is reported at $3,995.00 both before and after the 1 April 2026 change. That is consistent with the rule and must not change simply because occupancy changed.

occupancy_rows.rule: A 6.14 notice must be served on each subsequent occupant within a reasonable time after the landlord knows or should have known of the occupancy; sixty days is generally considered reasonable. Failure to serve it within 60 days of actual knowledge establishes a rebuttable presumption that it was not served within a reasonable time.
occupancy_rows.effect: The reported change was 1 April 2026, so the sixty-day benchmark fell around 31 May 2026, before this review. Whether a notice was served, and whether any presumption can be rebutted, is a private fact (H-23).

occupancy_rows.rule: Section 6.14(d)(2) states that the landlord is entitled to establish a new base rent under Costa-Hawkins even if no 6.14 notice was served on the subsequent occupant.
occupancy_rows.effect: A missed or late 6.14 notice does not by itself end the analysis. Costa-Hawkins has its own limits, including that it does not reach a co-tenant who moved in after the original occupant (H-24).

occupancy_rows.rule: A co-tenant is not subject to a Costa-Hawkins increase regardless of when the co-tenant moved in. A co-tenant is someone with an oral or written agreement with the landlord, or whom the landlord has treated as a tenant by the acceptance of rent or other conduct. A 6.14 notice, by contrast, can be served on either a subtenant or a co-tenant.
occupancy_rows.effect: If the incoming Unit 1 occupant was added to the lease, or the owner has accepted rent directly from them, they may be a co-tenant. That status is a private fact and changes which route, if any, is available later (H-24).

occupancy_rows.situation: No pre-filing is required for either route
occupancy_rows.rule: A landlord is not required to file a petition for approval of a §6.14 or Costa-Hawkins increase, but may file for a determination; a tenant may file a petition alleging an unlawful rent increase.
occupancy_rows.effect: If either route is ever relied on, the optional determination petition is a way to test it before serving. This dashboard does not establish that either route is available here.

occupancy_rows.situation: Effect on the annual and banked scenarios
occupancy_rows.rule: None of the above changes the 1.6% annual allowance while the current tenancies continue. It only matters if the last original occupant later leaves.
occupancy_rows.effect: Unit 1's reported scenarios stand as calculated. If the remaining original occupant later vacates, the analysis changes entirely and must be re-run from the records; do not reuse these figures.
